profile.address: 18844 FM 1957, San Antonio, Medina County, Texas, 78009
profile.reading:
This building sits in Medina County, Texas, in the area local reporting associates with Microsoft's SAT80 data center pair near Castroville, described by the San Antonio Report as two buildings each exceeding 106,000 square feet, sharing a roughly 206-acre rural site. Microsoft has built at least eight data centers across the San Antonio region, spanning Bexar and Medina counties, since first opening two facilities there in 2015 at roughly $90 million each; cumulative Microsoft investment in the region exceeded $1.2 billion as of August 2023. San Antonio's city council approved a 15-year Chapter 380 tax reimbursement in 2013 covering 40% of property taxes in exchange for a $250 million Microsoft investment commitment and the creation of 20 high-paying jobs, and Microsoft's subsequent expansion into rural Medina County reflects the same pattern of the company steadily broadening its San Antonio-area footprint well beyond its original commitment. Construction phases at Microsoft's San Antonio-area campuses have typically employed several hundred workers, while each completed data center building tends to run with a comparatively small operating staff of roughly 50 employees once online. Microsoft has not published this specific building's address, square footage, or MW capacity beyond what OSM and county records already provide, so this registry records the SAT80 pair's combined 106,000-plus-square-foot, 206-acre description as regional context rather than a confirmed fact for this exact structure.

CPS Energy, San Antonio's municipally owned electric and gas utility, the largest such public utility in the country, supplies power to Microsoft's San Antonio-area campuses and has cited large commercial and industrial customers, data centers among them, in its own integrated resource planning as it weighs new generation to meet growing demand. Because CPS Energy is municipally owned rather than investor-owned, large-load agreements with customers like Microsoft are negotiated directly with the city-owned utility rather than through the Public Utility Commission of Texas process that governs most of the state's investor-owned utilities.

reading.body:
Microsoft does not publish power capacity, square footage, or megawatt consumption for individual Azure data center campuses, including this San Antonio facility. The disclosure policy means this campus cannot be ranked or compared on the basis of computing density or grid load relative to other operators' facilities. Without published specifications, its contribution to AI scaling cannot be quantified from operator data.

The San Antonio region hosts a growing number of Microsoft data centers across Bexar and Medina counties, reflecting the company's continued expansion in Texas. Among 133 mapped facilities statewide, only 18 publish power consumption figures. This campus exists within that landscape but remains unquantified in the published data this site uses to assess grid constraints on AI.

The state context ranks this campus 19th in Texas by published MW, a meaningless ranking since Microsoft publishes no MW figure for it. The ranking reflects only that other operators have disclosed capacity at sites in the state. For readers assessing whether this campus matters to AI scaling, no published grid demand or compute density is available.
